faq.q: How does the anglerfish light work?
faq.a: A female anglerfish has a fishing-rod spine on her head tipped with a lure full of glowing bacteria. Small fish swim towards the light and she snaps them up.
asks: Why does the anglerfish have a light?

faq.q: Why do some fish glow on their bellies?
faq.a: In the twilight zone, a fish seen from below makes a dark shadow against the faint light above. Glowing belly lights fill in that shadow, so hunters cannot see it. This is called counter-illumination.

faq.q: Why is deep-sea light usually blue?
faq.a: Blue-green light travels farthest through seawater, while red light is soaked up within a few metres. So most deep-sea animals glow blue, and many cannot even see red.
asks: Why don't deep-sea animals glow red?

faq.q: How many deep-sea animals can glow?
faq.a: A lot. A study of ocean videos from the surface down to 4,000 metres found that about three quarters of the animals seen could make light.
asks: What percentage of sea animals glow?

faq.q: What else do sea animals use light for?
faq.a: They use it to attract prey, hide from predators, startle attackers, signal to mates and even light up the water like a torch. Some squid squirt glowing ink to escape.

facts: A 2017 study of ocean video found about 76 percent of animals observed between the surface and 4,000 metres could make light.
Blue-green light travels farthest through seawater, so most marine bioluminescence is blue-green.
Little usable sunlight reaches below about 1,000 metres in the open ocean.
